title: Vortex solitons in star networks
abstract: I consider vortex solitons in two-dimensional star networks created by several one-dimensional line waveguide arrays (or rays) brought in close proximity. First waveguide in each array belongs to the ring of certain radius and its modal field overlaps with modal fields of waveguides from other rays laying on this ring, as well as with modal fields of waveguides in this line array. This creates a system with discrete rotational symmetry that is capable of supporting various localized linear vortex states due to local coupling between waveguides on the central ring, where line arrays approach each other. Localized vortex states emerge from the continuum of the states extended along the rays of the structure upon variation of the radius of the central ring. I show how different vortex modes with progressively increasing topological charges emerge when the number of rays in structure and, therefore, its discrete rotational symmetry increases. Each such linear localized mode gives rise to a family of thresholdless vortex solitons in nonlinear optical medium, whose topological charges are limited by the discrete rotational symmetry of the system. Vortex solitons in star networks exhibit qualitatively different behavior with increasing power depending on whether the propagation constant of linear vortex that gives rise to a family of solitons is located above or below the band of extended states. Stability properties of vortex solitons nontrivially depend on their topological charge and discrete rotational symmetry of the system, showing very different picture from usual ring-like waveguide arrays.
summary: This work analyzes vortex solitons in complex star network waveguide arrays, demonstrating that the system's discrete rotational symmetry dictates the possible topological charges. The stability and existence of these solitons are critically dependent on how their associated linear modes interact with the extended state band of the structure. This reveals complex, symmetry-protected behavior distinct from simpler ring geometries.
main_problem: The paper investigates the existence, properties, and stability of vortex solitons within two-dimensional star networks formed by coupled line waveguide arrays.
main_result: The star networks support rich families of vortex solitons whose stability and behavior are highly dependent on the system's discrete rotational symmetry and whether the linear mode lies above or below the extended state band.
method: The analysis involves solving the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NSE) by first finding localized linear eigenmodes and then analyzing the stability of the resulting soliton solutions via direct evolution of perturbed fields.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a star network of coupled one-dimensional line waveguides, governed by a nonlinear wave equation. The structure's symmetry is controlled by the number of rays (N) and the central ring radius, tuned by a shift parameter (delta).
key_observables: Topological charge (m), soliton power (U), propagation constant (b), and stability (stable/unstable branches).
important_parameters: Number of rays (N), central ring radius (controlled by delta), and the relative position of the linear mode's propagation constant with respect to the extended state band.
main_assumptions: The waveguides are assumed to be Gaussian, and the analysis focuses on the case of a focusing nonlinear medium.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the refractive index profiles for different N and delta, show linear mode eigenvalues vs. delta, and map out the stability boundaries (U-b diagrams) for various vortex soliton families.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical system and linear modes to deriving the soliton solutions, and finally dedicating significant analysis to mapping out the stability properties of these vortex solitons, contrasting them with simpler ring geometries.
why_interesting: The study of topological defects (vortices) in structured nonlinear media, especially where the underlying linear spectrum has band gaps, is highly relevant to quantum optics and nonlinear wave physics, providing insights into robust information carriers.
